question: What exactly is water pollution?

options.A: The natural filtration of rainwater through soil layers
options.B: The contamination of water sources by harmful substances
options.C: The evaporation of clean water from surface reservoirs
options.D: The normal movement of minerals from rocks into rivers

explanation: Spot on! Water pollution happens when harmful agents find their way into natural water bodies, making them unsafe for use. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h1)

question: How does water pollution directly hurt everyday communities?

options.A: By speeding up the natural flow of underground aquifers
options.B: By lowering the overall temperature of local rivers
options.C: By increasing the mineral content of drinking water
options.D: By making available water sources unsafe for daily use

explanation: You got it! When water is contaminated, families can no longer use it safely for drinking, cooking, or basic hygiene, posing an immediate health threat. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h1)

question: Which of these counts as a biological water pollutant?
explanation: Great job! Biological pollutants are living germs or microorganisms, often introduced into water through waste contamination. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h2)

question: Where do most nutrient pollutants like nitrogen and phosphorus in water bodies come from?
explanation: Spot on! Fertilizers wash off farmlands during rains and flow into nearby streams and lakes, causing massive weed and algae growth. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h2)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a point source of water pollution?

options.A: Pesticides washing off multiple farms after a storm
options.B: General urban stormwater runoff from neighborhood streets
options.C: A factory discharge pipe leading directly into a river
options.D: Rainwater washing oil off a busy city highway

explanation: Correct! A point source has one clear, easy-to-spot origin, like a specific factory pipe or waste outlet. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h3)

question: Why are non-point sources of water pollution so tricky to control?

options.A: They originate from widespread, diffuse activities rather than a single pipe
options.B: They only occur deep underground where nurses cannot inspect them
options.C: They consist entirely of harmless organic materials that resist cleanup
options.D: They are strictly regulated and hidden by industrial factories

explanation: You nailed it! Because non-point pollution comes from vast areas like entire farming towns or busy streets, there is no single pipe to fix. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h3)

question: How do waterborne diseases like cholera and typhoid usually spread?

options.A: Inhalation of mist from clean cooling towers
options.B: Direct skin contact with industrial chemical waste
options.C: Mosquito bites near stagnant ponds and rivers
options.D: Ingestion of water contaminated with fecal matter

explanation: Correct! These nasty bugs spread mainly when people swallow food or water that has come into contact with human or animal waste. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h4)

question: A patient comes to your clinic with severe watery diarrhea and dehydration after drinking untreated stream water. What condition should you suspect?
explanation: Spot on, nurse! Severe diarrhea and rapid fluid loss after drinking unsafe water are classic signs of a bacterial infection like cholera. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h4)

question: What is eutrophication in plain terms?

options.A: A sudden increase of clean mineral nutrients in underground wells
options.B: The natural warming of river water by industrial thermal plants
options.C: Oxygen depletion in water caused by the decomposition of excess algae
options.D: The direct filtration of heavy metals through sandy soil layers

explanation: You got it! Too many nutrients cause massive algae blooms; when those plants die and rot, they suck all the oxygen out of the water. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h5)

question: What happens during biological magnification (biomagnification) in a food chain?

options.A: Microbiological pathogens are neutralized by natural river currents
options.B: Fish grow larger and healthier due to the presence of mineral nutrients
options.C: Algae populations decrease rapidly due to cold water temperatures
options.D: Toxic chemicals become more concentrated in predators at higher trophic levels

explanation: Correct! As small creatures eat toxins and get eaten by bigger fish and animals, the poison multiplies and gets stronger higher up the food chain. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h5)

question: Finding Escherichia coli (E. coli) in a water sample tells you what?

options.A: High concentrations of industrial heavy metals
options.B: Recent fecal contamination from humans or animals
options.C: Excessive mineral hardness from underground rocks
options.D: A normal and safe level of plant nutrients

explanation: Spot on! E. coli is our warning flag. Its presence proves that waste matter has found its way into the water supply. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h6)

question: Why do water quality testers measure turbidity?

options.A: To calculate the total mineral salt content in wells
options.B: To measure the exact temperature of the water source
options.C: To determine the amount of dissolved oxygen available
options.D: To check how cloudy the water is from suspended particles

explanation: Great job! Turbidity just means cloudiness. High cloudiness is dangerous because it hides harmful germs from water treatment chemicals. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h6)

question: What is the main goal of the preliminary stage in wastewater treatment?

options.A: Killing all microscopic bacteria using chlorine gas
options.B: Adding oxygen to stimulate helpful aerobic microbes
options.C: Filtering out dissolved chemical salts and heavy metals
options.D: Removing large physical objects like plastics and rags

explanation: You got it! Before treating water, we have to screen out big trash like nylons and plastics so they don't break the treatment machinery. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h7)

question: Which wastewater treatment stage uses helpful oxygen-loving bacteria to break down organic waste?
explanation: Spot on! Secondary treatment brings in oxygen and good microbes to literally eat up and clean out the dissolved waste particles. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h7)

question: As a nurse, what simple and effective practice should you teach community members in areas with unsafe water?

options.A: Avoiding all handwashing to save clean water
options.B: Using untreated river water for infant formula
options.D: Adding industrial solvents to kill local algae

explanation: Correct! Boiling is a cheap, reliable way families can kill germs at home when tap or well water isn't safe. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h8)

question: You are deployed to a rural village experiencing a sudden cholera outbreak. What should be your immediate nursing priority?

options.A: Instructing residents to swim only in stagnant agricultural ponds
options.B: Administering broad-spectrum topical creams to all affected skin areas
options.C: Collecting industrial factory waste samples from local rivers
options.D: Providing oral rehydration therapy and promoting safe drinking water practices

explanation: Brilliant! Saving lives means stopping dehydration right away with oral rehydration therapy and making sure patients stop drinking contaminated water. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h8)
